The goal of this project is to predict an individual's Pulse using the NHANES
training data. This notebook documents the analysis of demographic, health, and lifestyle
variables associated with resting pulse rate.

## 1. Load the training data

The training data are stored in the repository `data/` directory.
```{r}
nhanes <- read.csv("data/NHANES-training.csv")
```

Check the number of rows and columns in the imported data:

```{r}
dim(nhanes)
```

## 2. Checking Variables

I first checked candidate predictors for missingness and variability, then examined their relationships with Pulse. The initial summaries below document screening before the exclusions.

```{r}
variables <- c(
  "Pulse",
  "Gender", "Age", "Race1", "Education", "MaritalStatus",
  "HHIncome", "Poverty", "Work",
  "BMI", "BPSysAve", "BPDiaAve", "Testosterone", "DirectChol", "TotChol",
  "Diabetes", "HealthGen", "DaysPhysHlthBad", "DaysMentHlthBad",
  "SleepHrsNight", "SleepTrouble",
  "PhysActive", "PhysActiveDays", "TVHrsDay", "CompHrsDay",
  "Alcohol12PlusYr", "AlcoholDay", "AlcoholYear", "Smoke100", "SmokeNow"
)
```

Check the percentage of missing values.
```{r}
round(colMeans(is.na(nhanes[variables])) * 100, 1)
```


Check the numerical variables for their ranges, unusual values, and variability.
```{r}
numerical <- c(
  "Pulse", "Age", "Poverty", "BMI", "BPSysAve", "BPDiaAve",
  "Testosterone", "DirectChol", "TotChol", "DaysPhysHlthBad",
  "DaysMentHlthBad", "SleepHrsNight", "PhysActiveDays",
  "AlcoholDay", "AlcoholYear"
)

summary(nhanes[numerical])
```

I excluded PhysActiveDays and AlcoholDay from the initial predictor list because they were missing 52.7% and 33.3% of their values, respectively. I retained PhysActive as a more complete measure of physical activity. I considered Alcohol12PlusYr and AlcoholYear as alternative alcohol measures. Rather than exclude smoking information, I combined Smoke100 and SmokeNow.

```{r}
nhanes$SmokeStatus <- ifelse(
  nhanes$Smoke100 == "No", "Under100",
  ifelse(nhanes$SmokeNow == "Yes", "Current", "Former")
)

table(nhanes$SmokeStatus)
```
Here, Under100 means fewer than 100 lifetime cigarettes. Current and Former refer to participants who reported smoking at least 100 lifetime cigarettes.

SmokeStatus replaces the two original smoking variables in subsequent EDA.



Count observations in each category of the categorical variables.
```{r}
categorical <- c(
  "Gender", "Race1", "Education", "MaritalStatus", "HHIncome",
  "Work", "Diabetes", "HealthGen", "SleepTrouble", "PhysActive",
  "TVHrsDay", "CompHrsDay", "Alcohol12PlusYr", "SmokeStatus"
)

lapply(nhanes[categorical], table, useNA = "ifany")
```

## 3. Distribution of Pulse

```{r}
library(mosaic)
library(ggformula)

favstats(~Pulse, data = nhanes)

gf_histogram(~Pulse, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Pulse is unimodal and slightly right-skewed. The mean is 72.62 beats per minute and the median is 72. The middle 50% of values lie between 64 and 80, with a full range of 40 to 136. The value of 136 is separated from the main cluster. It was retained because the available information does not establish a recording error; unusual values require separate review. There are 47 missing Pulse values.

## 4. Distributions of Numerical Predictors

PhysActiveDays and AlcoholDay were excluded during the initial missingness screening. The retained numerical predictors are:

```{r}
numerical <- c(
  "Age", "Poverty", "BMI", "BPSysAve", "BPDiaAve",
  "Testosterone", "DirectChol", "TotChol", "DaysPhysHlthBad",
  "DaysMentHlthBad", "SleepHrsNight", "AlcoholYear"
)
```

### Age

```{r}
favstats(~Age, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~Age, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Recorded Age is broadly distributed across adulthood rather than bell-shaped. The mean of the recorded values is 47.40 years and the median is 47. The middle 50% lie between 33 and 61, with a recorded range of 20 to 80. The 87 observations coded as 80 represent participants aged 80 or older, consistent with the reported age coding.

### Poverty

```{r}
favstats(~Poverty, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~Poverty, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Poverty has an irregular distribution with a large spike at 5. The mean is 2.89 and the median is 2.86. The middle 50% of values lie between 1.33 and 4.89, with a full range of 0 to 5. The 400 observations equal to 5 represent ratios of 5 or higher. This concentration reflects a reporting limit.

### BMI

```{r}
favstats(~BMI, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~BMI, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

BMI is unimodal and right-skewed. The mean is 28.71 and the median is 27.70. The middle 50% of values lie between 23.90 and 32.20, with a full range of 15.70 to 69.00. Values such as 59.20, 62.80, and 69.00 are far above the main cluster. I retained them because the available information does not establish recording errors; their influence can be examined during model evaluation.

### Average systolic blood pressure

```{r}
favstats(~BPSysAve, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~BPSysAve, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Average systolic blood pressure is unimodal and right-skewed. The mean is 121.28 mm Hg and the median is 119. The middle 50% of readings lie between 110 and 130, with a full range of 81 to 221. Readings around 202 and the maximum of 221 are unusually high compared with the main cluster. I retained them, with their possible influence noted for model evaluation.

### Average diastolic blood pressure

```{r}
favstats(~BPDiaAve, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~BPDiaAve, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Most average diastolic blood pressure readings form a roughly symmetric, unimodal cluster around 72 mm Hg, but low readings create a longer left tail. The mean is 71.34 mm Hg and the median is 72. The middle 50% lie between 65 and 78, with a full range of 0 to 107. Five observations equal 0. I examined their recorded readings and retained the supplied averages, for further examination.

### Testosterone

```{r}
favstats(~Testosterone, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~Testosterone, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Testosterone has a large concentration of low values and a broader second concentration at several hundred ng/dL, with a long right tail. The mean is 217.83 ng/dL and the median is approximately 91.73. The middle 50% of values lie between 19.89 and 378.33, with a full range of 1.79 to 1795.60. The largest readings, especially 1795.60, were flagged and retained, for further examination. Gender-specific distributions may explain the two concentrations.

### HDL cholesterol

```{r}
favstats(~DirectChol, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~DirectChol, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

HDL cholesterol is unimodal and right-skewed. The mean is 1.36 mmol/L and the median is 1.29. The middle 50% of readings lie between 1.09 and 1.58, with a full range of 0.47 to 3.83. Readings around 3.59 and the maximum of 3.83 are unusually high compared with most observations. They were flagged and retained, for further examination.

### Total cholesterol

```{r}
favstats(~TotChol, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~TotChol, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Total cholesterol is unimodal and slightly right-skewed, with a few high readings extending the right tail. The mean is 5.01 mmol/L and the median is 4.91. The middle 50% of readings lie between 4.27 and 5.66, with a full range of 2.17 to 12.28. Readings of 10.29 and 12.28 are far above the main cluster. They were flagged and retained, for further examination.

### Days of poor physical health

```{r}
favstats(~DaysPhysHlthBad, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~DaysPhysHlthBad, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Days of poor physical health is strongly right-skewed, with most participants reporting 0 days and a smaller spike at 30 days. The mean is 3.39 days and the median is 0. The middle 50% of values lie between 0 and 2, with a full range of 0 to 30. Although 30 days is far from the main concentration, it falls within the question's reporting period and should not automatically be treated as an error.

### Days of poor mental health

```{r}
favstats(~DaysMentHlthBad, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~DaysMentHlthBad, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Days of poor mental health is strongly right-skewed, with most participants reporting 0 days and a smaller spike at 30 days. The mean is 3.95 days and the median is 0. The middle 50% of values lie between 0 and 4, with a full range of 0 to 30. Reports of 30 days are relatively high but fall within the reporting period, so they should not automatically be removed.

### Hours of sleep per night

```{r}
favstats(~SleepHrsNight, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~SleepHrsNight, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Hours of sleep has a roughly symmetric overall distribution concentrated at 6, 7, and 8 hours, with 8 hours the most frequent response. The mean is 6.88 hours and the median is 7. The middle 50% of values lie between 6 and 8, with a full range of 2 to 12. Reports of 2 and 12 hours are unusual compared with the main cluster. They were flagged and retained, for further examination.

### Drinking days per year

```{r}
favstats(~AlcoholYear, data = nhanes)
gf_histogram(~AlcoholYear, data = nhanes, bins = 30)
```

Drinking days per year is strongly right-skewed, with many observations near 0 and spikes at values such as 12, 24, 52, and 104. The mean is 75.75 days and the median is 24. The middle 50% of values lie between 3 and 104, with a full range of 0 to 364. Values near 364 are far from most observations but remain within a year. The spikes indicate repeated reported or derived drinking frequencies. I retained the supplied values without reconstructing the underlying responses.

### Unusual values

I flagged unusual values and left the original measurements unchanged. A later review will document the coding checks for Age, Poverty, and zero diastolic readings. Extreme values alone were not sufficient grounds for removing observations.


## 5. Distributions of Categorical Predictors

Percentages exclude missing responses. The frequency tables in Section 2 report missing values separately. The graphs below show recorded categories.

### Gender

```{r}
gf_bar(~Gender, data = nhanes)
```

Gender is almost evenly divided: 907 participants are female (50.2%) and 900 are male (49.8%). Both categories have many observations, and there are no missing values.

### Race

```{r}
gf_bar(~Race1, data = nhanes)
```

White is the most common category, containing 1,200 participants (66.4%). The remaining categories are Black (10.3%), Other (8.6%), Mexican (7.9%), and Hispanic (6.8%). The categories are unevenly distributed, but each contains more than 100 observations.

### Education

```{r}
gf_bar(~Education, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(Education))) +
  coord_flip()
```

College graduates (32.4%) and participants with some college education (31.7%) are the largest groups. High school graduates account for 18.3%, followed by grades 9–11 (11.1%) and the 8th-grade category (6.5%). Every category has more than 100 observations. There are three missing responses.

### Marital status

```{r}
gf_bar(~MaritalStatus, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(MaritalStatus))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Married participants form the largest group (53.2%), followed by participants who have never married (21.4%). The remaining categories are divorced (10.1%), living with a partner (7.3%), widowed (5.7%), and separated (2.3%). Separated is the smallest category, with 42 observations, so comparisons involving this group may be less precise. There are two missing responses.

### Household income

```{r}
gf_bar(~HHIncome, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(HHIncome))) +
  coord_flip()
```

The largest household income category is $100,000 or more, containing 418 participants (25.2% of those with reported income). The smallest categories are $0–$4,999, with 37 observations, and $5,000–$9,999, with 41. The remaining participants are spread across the other income categories. There are 149 missing responses. The smaller groups may need consideration when deciding how to represent income in the model.

### Work status

```{r}
gf_bar(~Work, data = nhanes)
```

Most participants are working (60.4%), followed by those not working (35.7%). Only 69 participants (3.8%) are looking for work. The Looking category is much smaller than the other two categories and may produce less precise comparisons. There are no missing responses.

### Diabetes

```{r}
gf_bar(~Diabetes, data = nhanes)
```

Most participants report no diabetes: 1,613 (89.3%) answered No and 194 (10.7%) answered Yes. Although the categories are uneven, the Yes group still contains a substantial number of observations. There are no missing responses.

### General health

```{r}
gf_bar(~HealthGen, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(HealthGen)))
```

Good (39.8%) and very good (32.7%) are the most common health ratings. Fair accounts for 13.4%, excellent for 11.7%, and poor for 2.4%. Poor is the smallest category, with 39 observations, so comparisons involving this group should be interpreted carefully. There are 164 missing responses.

### Trouble sleeping

```{r}
gf_bar(~SleepTrouble, data = nhanes)
```

A total of 512 participants (28.3%) report having told a health professional about trouble sleeping, while 1,295 (71.7%) do not. Both categories contain many observations. There are no missing responses.

### Physical activity

```{r}
gf_bar(~PhysActive, data = nhanes)
```

Slightly more than half of participants report moderate or vigorous recreational activity: 1,002 (55.5%) answered Yes and 805 (44.5%) answered No. The categories are reasonably balanced, and there are no missing responses.

### Television hours per day

```{r}
gf_bar(~TVHrsDay, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(TVHrsDay)))
```

The most common response is 2 hours per day (26.3%), followed by 3 hours (17.4%). The smallest category is 0 hours, with 40 observations (2.2%). Participants are otherwise distributed across several viewing-time categories. There is one missing response.

### Computer or gaming hours per day

```{r}
gf_bar(~CompHrsDay, data = nhanes)
```

The most common response is more than 0 but less than 1 hour per day (28.3%), followed by 0 hours (22.5%) and 1 hour (20.0%). Higher-use categories generally contain fewer participants. The smallest category is 4 hours, with 73 observations (4.0%). There are no missing responses.

### Alcohol: at least 12 drinks in any one year

```{r}
gf_bar(~Alcohol12PlusYr, data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(Alcohol12PlusYr)))
```

Among participants with a recorded response, 1,300 (79.4%) report consuming at least 12 alcoholic drinks in any one year, while 338 (20.6%) do not. Both categories contain many observations, although Yes is substantially more common. There are 169 missing responses.

### Smoking status

```{r}
gf_bar(~SmokeStatus, data = nhanes)
```

The largest group consists of participants who have smoked fewer than 100 lifetime cigarettes: 1,009 participants (55.8%). Former smokers account for 451 participants (25.0%), and current smokers account for 347 (19.2%). The Current and Former categories refer to participants who reported smoking at least 100 lifetime cigarettes. All three groups contain many observations, and the combined variable has no missing values.

### Decisions from the categorical distributions

I retained the categorical predictors for examination against Pulse. Several categories are relatively small, particularly Separated, Poor general health, the lowest income groups, and zero television hours. After examining their relationships with Pulse, I retained these categories, subject to separate coding review. Unequal category sizes alone do not establish whether a predictor is useful.

## 6. Relationships Between Numerical Predictors and Pulse

I used scatterplots to examine direction, form, strength, and unusual observations. Correlations were calculated using observations with both variables recorded.

### Age and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ Age, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$Age, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is a weak negative relationship between Age and Pulse (r = -0.19). Older participants generally have lower pulse rates, although pulse varies considerably at every age. The overall pattern is approximately linear. Age is worth considering during model building.

### Poverty and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ Poverty, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$Poverty, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is a weak negative relationship between Poverty and Pulse (r = -0.10). Higher income-to-poverty ratios tend to be associated with slightly lower pulse rates, but the points are widely scattered. The concentration at a ratio of 5 produces a vertical stack of observations.

### BMI and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ BMI, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$BMI, use = "complete.obs")
```

The overall linear relationship between BMI and Pulse is weak and positive (r = 0.10). Pulse tends to be somewhat higher among participants with higher BMI, but the pattern is not a clear straight line. The largest BMI values are isolated from most observations and could influence a fitted relationship. BMI is worth further consideration, including checking whether its relationship with Pulse is curved.

### Systolic blood pressure and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ BPSysAve, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$BPSysAve, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is little evidence of an overall linear relationship between systolic blood pressure and Pulse (r = -0.04). Pulse varies widely across the observed blood pressure readings. A few unusually high systolic readings are separated from the main cluster. This variable appears less promising when examined on its own.

### Diastolic blood pressure and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ BPDiaAve, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$BPDiaAve, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is a weak positive relationship between diastolic blood pressure and Pulse (r = 0.13), with considerable scatter. Higher diastolic readings tend to accompany slightly higher pulse rates. The five zero readings are separated from the main cluster. Their coding was investigated and the supplied averages were retained, subject to separate coding review.

### Testosterone and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ Testosterone, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$Testosterone, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is a weak negative overall linear relationship between Testosterone and Pulse (r = -0.13). The observations are unevenly distributed, with many low testosterone readings and a broad range of pulse rates. The pattern is not well summarized by a single straight line. The comparison with Gender in Section 9 provides context for this pooled relationship.

### HDL cholesterol and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ DirectChol, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$DirectChol, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is almost no overall linear relationship between HDL cholesterol and Pulse (r = -0.02). The scatterplot has no clear upward or downward trend. A few high HDL readings are isolated from the main cluster and were retained for further coding review. HDL cholesterol appears less promising as an individual predictor.

### Total cholesterol and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ TotChol, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$TotChol, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is almost no overall linear relationship between total cholesterol and Pulse (r = 0.03). Pulse varies substantially across cholesterol readings, without a clear trend. The highest cholesterol readings are isolated and were retained for further coding review. Total cholesterol appears less promising when considered alone.

### Days of poor physical health and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ DaysPhysHlthBad, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$DaysPhysHlthBad, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is little overall linear relationship between days of poor physical health and Pulse (r = -0.03). Many observations occur at 0 days, and pulse rates vary widely within this group. The remaining observations do not show a consistent upward or downward pattern.

### Days of poor mental health and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ DaysMentHlthBad, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$DaysMentHlthBad, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is a weak positive relationship between days of poor mental health and Pulse (r = 0.10). Participants reporting more days of poor mental health tend to have slightly higher pulse rates, although there is substantial scatter. The large concentration at 0 days and smaller numbers at many other values should be considered when interpreting the pattern.

### Hours of sleep and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ SleepHrsNight, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$SleepHrsNight, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is essentially no overall linear relationship between hours of sleep and Pulse (r = -0.01). Pulse rates vary widely within the common sleep durations of 6, 7, and 8 hours. Very short and very long sleep durations have few observations, making their patterns difficult to assess.

### Drinking days per year and Pulse

```{r}
gf_point(Pulse ~ AlcoholYear, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$Pulse, nhanes$AlcoholYear, use = "complete.obs")
```

There is almost no overall linear relationship between drinking days per year and Pulse (r = -0.01). Pulse rates are spread widely across drinking frequencies, without a consistent trend. Combined with its 19.1% missingness, this makes AlcoholYear a lower-priority candidate based on the initial EDA.

## 7. Relationships Between Categorical Predictors and Pulse

I used side-by-side boxplots and grouped numerical summaries to compare Pulse across categories. The reported means use participants with recorded Pulse and a recorded predictor category. Differences between groups describe associations and do not establish causation.

### Gender and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Gender, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Gender, data = nhanes)
```

Female participants have a higher mean pulse than male participants: 73.71 compared with 71.53 beats per minute. Their medians are 74 and 70, respectively. The distributions overlap substantially, but the difference in their centers makes Gender worth considering.

### Race and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Race1, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Race1, data = nhanes)
```

Mean pulse rates range from 71.79 in the Black category to 73.97 in the Other category. Most category medians are close to 72, and the distributions overlap substantially. Race1 shows relatively small differences in Pulse when examined alone.

### Education and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Education, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Education,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(Education))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Mean pulse differs across education categories. It is lowest in the 8thGrade category at 70.04 and highest in SomeCollege at 73.73 beats per minute. College graduates have a mean of 71.53. The distributions overlap, and the differences do not follow a simple increasing or decreasing educational pattern. Education is worth examining alongside Age.

### Marital status and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ MaritalStatus, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ MaritalStatus,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(MaritalStatus))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Participants who have never married have a mean pulse of 75.15, compared with 71.26 among married participants. Participants living with a partner also have a relatively high mean of 74.37. The distributions overlap, but the differences in centers make MaritalStatus worth considering. Its relationship with Age should also be examined.

### Household income and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ HHIncome, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ HHIncome,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(HHIncome))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Mean pulse differs across income categories, but there is no consistent step-by-step pattern. For example, the mean is 74.63 in the $20,000–$24,999 category, 69.31 in the $65,000–$74,999 category, and 71.03 in the $100,000-or-more category. The distributions overlap substantially. Income should be examined alongside Poverty because they describe related economic circumstances.

### Work status and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Work, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Work, data = nhanes)
```

Participants looking for work have the highest mean pulse at 74.06, followed by those not working at 73.09 and those working at 72.25. The differences are small relative to the variation within each group. Only 65 participants in the Looking category have recorded Pulse, so comparisons involving this group are less precise.

### Diabetes and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Diabetes, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Diabetes, data = nhanes)
```

Participants reporting diabetes have a slightly higher mean pulse than those without diabetes: 73.84 compared with 72.47. Both groups have a median of 72, and their distributions overlap substantially. Diabetes shows only a small unadjusted difference in Pulse.

### General health and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ HealthGen, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ HealthGen,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(HealthGen)))
```

Mean pulse rates are similar across general-health categories, ranging from 71.97 for very good health to 73.59 for fair health. There is no consistent increase in Pulse as reported health becomes worse. The Poor category has only 39 observations and a relatively wide spread, so its summary is less stable.

### Trouble sleeping and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ SleepTrouble, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ SleepTrouble, data = nhanes)
```

Participants reporting trouble sleeping have a mean pulse of 73.03, compared with 72.45 among those who do not. Both groups have a median of 72, and their distributions are very similar. SleepTrouble shows little separation in Pulse when examined alone.

### Physical activity and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ PhysActive, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ PhysActive, data = nhanes)
```

Physically active and inactive participants have very similar pulse distributions. Their means are 72.74 and 72.46, respectively, and both groups have a median of 72. The boxplots show little unadjusted association between this activity measure and Pulse.

### Television hours and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ TVHrsDay, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ TVHrsDay,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(TVHrsDay)))
```

Participants watching more than 4 hours of television per day have a mean pulse of 74.40, compared with 71.40 among those watching 1 hour and 71.03 among those watching 3 hours. The distributions overlap, and the pattern is not consistently increasing across categories. Higher viewing categories show some differences worth further examination.

### Computer or gaming hours and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ CompHrsDay, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ CompHrsDay, data = nhanes)
```

Mean pulse generally increases across computer or gaming time categories, from 71.68 among participants reporting 0 hours to 74.84 among those reporting more than 4 hours. The distributions overlap considerably, so the association is modest. This variable is worth examining alongside Age and the other predictors.

### Alcohol history and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ Alcohol12PlusYr, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ Alcohol12PlusYr,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(Alcohol12PlusYr)))
```

Participants reporting at least 12 drinks in any one year have a mean pulse of 72.45, compared with 73.31 among those answering No. Both groups have a median of 72, and their distributions overlap substantially. This variable shows only a small unadjusted difference in Pulse.

### Smoking status and Pulse

```{r}
favstats(Pulse ~ SmokeStatus, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Pulse ~ SmokeStatus, data = nhanes)
```

Current smokers have a mean pulse of 73.65, compared with 72.23 among former smokers and 72.44 among participants who have smoked fewer than 100 lifetime cigarettes. All three groups have a median of 72, and the distributions overlap substantially. Smoking status shows a modest difference in group means that can be considered alongside other predictors.

## 8. Initial Conclusions From the Predictor–Pulse Comparisons

None of the numerical predictors shows a strong individual linear relationship with Pulse. Age has the clearest overall linear trend, while Poverty, BMI, diastolic blood pressure, Testosterone, and days of poor mental health show weaker patterns worth investigating further.

Among the categorical predictors, Gender, Education, MaritalStatus, and computer or gaming hours show differences in group centers worth further examination. Television hours, smoking status, and household income also show some differences, although their distributions overlap substantially.

These comparisons provide an initial guide rather than a final selection. A predictor with a weak individual relationship may still contribute when considered with other variables. These comparisons motivate a later review of relationships among predictors and the EDA shortlist.


## 9. Relationships Between Predictors

I examined selected predictor relationships to identify overlapping information, group differences, and patterns that may matter during model building. Each comparison uses observations with the relevant variables recorded.

### Age, BMI, and blood pressure

```{r}
pairs(~Age + BMI + BPSysAve + BPDiaAve, data = nhanes)

cor(nhanes[c("Age", "BMI", "BPSysAve", "BPDiaAve")],
    use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
```

Age and systolic blood pressure have a moderate positive relationship (r = 0.42): older participants generally have higher systolic readings. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure also have a moderate positive relationship (r = 0.36), although the readings are far from perfectly related.

The relationship between Age and diastolic blood pressure appears curved, with readings generally rising into middle adulthood and then declining at older ages. Its near-zero linear correlation therefore does not fully describe the pattern. BMI has relatively weak linear relationships with Age and the two blood pressure measures.

These relationships suggest that age and blood pressure should be considered together. The five zero diastolic readings were investigated and retained, subject to separate coding review.

### Household income and Poverty

```{r}
favstats(Poverty ~ HHIncome, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Poverty ~ HHIncome,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(HHIncome))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Poverty ratios generally increase across higher household income categories. The median ratio rises from 0.13 in the lowest income category to 5.00 in the highest category. This shows substantial overlap in the economic information represented by HHIncome and Poverty.

The measures use different definitions and are not interchangeable. However, including both may add complexity without much additional information. The modeling stage should compare their contributions rather than automatically include both.

### Gender and Testosterone

```{r}
favstats(Testosterone ~ Gender, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Testosterone ~ Gender, data = nhanes)
```

Testosterone differs substantially between the Gender groups. The median is 19.88 ng/dL among female participants and 377.90 ng/dL among male participants. Male participants also have a much wider spread.

These group differences help explain the two concentrations in the overall Testosterone distribution. Its relationship with Pulse should therefore be examined alongside Gender. The pooled negative association between Testosterone and Pulse may not describe the relationship within each group.

### Age and Education

```{r}
favstats(Age ~ Education, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Age ~ Education,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(Education))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Age distributions differ across education categories. Participants in the 8thGrade category have a median age of 60, compared with 43 among those with some college education and 46 among college graduates.

Because Age is associated with Pulse, some differences in Pulse across education categories could reflect differences in age composition. Education should therefore be considered alongside Age before interpreting its contribution.

### Age and Marital status

```{r}
favstats(Age ~ MaritalStatus, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Age ~ MaritalStatus,
           data = subset(nhanes, !is.na(MaritalStatus))) +
  coord_flip()
```

Age differs considerably across marital-status categories. The median age is 28 among participants who have never married, 49.5 among married participants, and 74 among widowed participants.

Participants who have never married also had a higher average Pulse than married participants. Their younger age distribution could partly account for that difference. I should assess whether MaritalStatus provides additional information after accounting for Age.

### Age and Work status

```{r}
favstats(Age ~ Work, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Age ~ Work, data = nhanes)
```

Participants who are not working tend to be older. Their median age is 61, compared with 43 among working participants and 38 among those looking for work.

Work status therefore contains information related to Age. Differences in Pulse across work categories should be interpreted with these age differences in mind.

### Age and Computer or gaming hours

```{r}
favstats(Age ~ CompHrsDay, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Age ~ CompHrsDay, data = nhanes)
```

Participants reporting no computer or gaming time tend to be older, with a median age of 58. The median is 42.5 among those reporting 1 hour, 28 among those reporting 4 hours, and 37 among those reporting more than 4 hours.

The age pattern is not perfectly consistent across categories, but higher-use groups generally contain younger participants. This could partly explain their higher average Pulse, since younger participants tend to have higher pulse rates.

### Age and Diabetes

```{r}
favstats(Age ~ Diabetes, data = nhanes)
gf_boxplot(Age ~ Diabetes, data = nhanes)
```

Participants reporting diabetes tend to be older. Their median age is 61, compared with 44 among participants without diabetes.

Because Age is associated with both diabetes status and Pulse, the small unadjusted difference in Pulse between diabetes groups may change when Age is considered. Diabetes should not be judged solely from its individual comparison with Pulse.

### BMI and HDL cholesterol

```{r}
gf_point(DirectChol ~ BMI, data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)
cor(nhanes$DirectChol, nhanes$BMI, use = "complete.obs")
```

BMI and HDL cholesterol have a moderate negative relationship (r = -0.36). Participants with higher BMI generally have lower HDL cholesterol, although there is considerable scatter.

The variables contain some related information, but the association is not strong enough to treat them as interchangeable. Their contributions to predicting Pulse would need to be evaluated together.

### Physical and mental health days

```{r}
gf_point(DaysMentHlthBad ~ DaysPhysHlthBad,
         data = nhanes, alpha = 0.5)

cor(nhanes$DaysMentHlthBad, nhanes$DaysPhysHlthBad,
    use = "complete.obs")
```

Days of poor physical and mental health have a weak positive relationship (r = 0.22). Participants reporting more days of poor physical health tend to report somewhat more days of poor mental health, but the observations are widely scattered.

Many participants report zero days for one or both measures. The two variables capture related aspects of health but do not provide identical information.

### Implications for the EDA shortlist

Age is related to several other predictors, particularly MaritalStatus, Work, Education, computer or gaming hours, and Diabetes. Their individual relationships with Pulse may therefore differ from their relationships after accounting for Age.

HHIncome and Poverty show substantial overlap, while Gender and Testosterone also share considerable information. These combinations deserve attention when choosing an effective set of predictors. Moderate associations, such as those between the blood pressure measures or between BMI and HDL cholesterol, do not by themselves justify removing a variable.
